Rounds of showers and breezy periods will follow early Sunday and Monday mornings, with isolated to scattered showers and a chance of thunderstorms in between. Warm and humid conditions on Sunday will trend much cooler and drier on Monday.
A progressive pattern will support periods of rain showers with a trough favored to move through Tuesday night into Wednesday.

Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Burlington VT
126 AM EDT Sat Sep 12 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
As of 217 PM EDT Friday...

Chances for showers early Sunday morning in southern portions 
of the region have increased. Confidence in isolated to 
scattered showers and a few thunderstorms for late Sunday has 
increased slightly. Temperatures for Monday have decreased. 
Winds and precipitation chances for Tuesday/Tuesday night have 
decreased.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
As of 217 PM EDT Friday...

1. Dry, clear, and seasonably cool weather will continue 
through Saturday, supporting our coolest morning of the season 
so far. 

2. Rounds of showers and breezy periods will follow early 
Sunday and Monday mornings, with isolated to scattered showers 
and a chance of thunderstorms in between. Warm and humid 
conditions on Sunday will trend much cooler and drier on Monday.


3. A progressive pattern will support periods of rain showers 
with a trough favored to move through Tuesday night into 
Wednesday.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
As of 217 PM EDT Friday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: High pressure will dominate the first part of 
the weekend. Aside from diurnally driven cumulus, an expansive 
area of cloud-free skies is noted on satellite imagery today 
across the Northeast and Great Lakes regions, which increases 
confidence in quiet weather continuing through tomorrow as the 
center of high pressure drifts to our east. This scenario will 
lead to a large swing in temperature from sunrise to midday. 
Morning temperatures in our region are on track to be the 
coolest we have seen since June 3rd. Here in Burlington, a low 
temperature below 50 is expected. That would end a string of 
exactly 100 days with a minimum temperature of 50 or higher, 
which is the second longest streak on record (longest is 106 
days three years ago). With increasing southerly flow during the
day and abundant sunshine, temperatures should surge following 
the dissipation of river valley fog, topping out in the mid to 
upper 70s for most locations. These temperatures are a few 
degrees above normal.

KEY MESSAGE 2: While no significant impacts are expected, an 
active period of weather appears to be headed our way from 
Saturday night through Monday morning. Three distinct chances 
for showers in portions of our region are anticipated associated
with different fronts. 

The first one will be tied to a wave of low pressure passing 
well to our south. There have been indications of this system 
for a few days and the latest guidance seems to be in excellent 
agreement on a slug of moisture and some elevated instability 
tracking into southern Vermont by midnight. An upper level 
shortwave passing to its north may aid in more widespread 
coverage of showers, which leads to uncertainty in how far north
higher PoPs should be. Generally risk of heavier showers and 
perhaps a rumble of thunder looks relegated to our southern 
areas in Vermont, but at least some shower activity is 
increasingly likely in much if not all of Vermont and northern 
New York at some point in the overnight hours. Measurable rain 
is greatly favored for central/southern Vermont and the southern
Champlain Valley. Total rainfall during this period will be 
variable, with mainly light amounts under 0.25" along with 
localized pockets of near or a bit above 0.5". Alongside the 
showers, a fairly potent low level jet will translate 
northeastward through the region, with strongest 850 millibar 
flow likely staying in the southern Vermont areas producing 
brisk mountain summit winds. However, localized valley 
channeling of southerly (or southwesterly in the St. Lawrence 
Valley) winds are favored areawide. There is a strong consensus 
of 30+ knot winds over the eastern portion of Lake Champlain 
through much of the Sunday morning hours.

The second round of showers will be tied to the lead cold front
approaching from the west midday Sunday. The timing of this 
boundary along with modest height falls will result in marginal 
instability to support slight chances for late afternoon and 
evening thunderstorms. The risk of thunderstorms should 
generally shift eastward through this period from northeastern 
New York to northeastern Vermont; probabilistic hazard guidance 
is in fairly good consensus that suggests thunderstorms are 
likely in the region but with a low chance for any particular 
location given the limited instability. The isolated risk of a 
stronger variety thunderstorm also is present, driven by a 
severe wind risk amidst 40-50 knots of deep layer shear with 
veering profiles and greatly increasing speeds with height. The 
Day 3 Severe Weather Outlook currently is in the 1 out 5 
category (isolated severe storms possible) for most of our 
region coinciding with this potential event; given the progged 
instability being modest (mixed layer CAPE around 500 J/kg) and 
limited coverage of thunderstorms amidst dry air aloft, would 
expect the outlook risk level will not increase as we get 
closer.

The final round of showers will be tied to a vigorous shortwave
trough that helps bring in a surge of colder/drier air into our
region early Monday morning. This forcing is stronger that the 
surface cold front, so while the potential for heavy rainfall is
low, the rain during this period may be relatively widespread 
and shallow instability should lead to brief downpours. Have 
noted precipitation chances have come up, but the likely 
scenario supports only upwards of an hour or two of rain 
occurring at any one location. With uncertainty in timing of 
these showers, the broad-brushed PoPs will need to be fine tuned
as it becomes more clear how the showers will progress through 
the region.

Monday then will trend dry as high pressure with origins in 
northwestern Canada will build in. Have noted that the latest 
guidance has 850 millibar temperatures only in the 2 to 3 
Celsius range during the day on Monday, or a bit lower than what
we are seeing today. If this verifies, high temperatures will 
be even lower than the current forecast with valleys only 
reaching the low to mid 60s even with deep mixing.

KEY MESSAGE 3: 500 mb flow in the mid-high latitudes are 
favored to be mainly zonal with Arctic air trapped well north of
the region. Fast- moving troughs will be moving through this 
flow with model trends maintaining a weaker wave passing Tuesday
night into Wednesday. The biggest question is whether or not a 
quasi-stationary boundary with linger over portions of northern 
New York and Vermont through the end of the week. Latest trends 
point to a more southerly push over what was presented in 
guidance yesterday, so this would lead to lower chances of 
prolonged precipitation. This is reflected in WPC probabilities 
of rain chances mid/late next week generally in the 20- 40% 
range outside of the next wave moving through. The next wave 
approaches Thursday and may result in increasing precipitation 
chances once models consolidate around wave timing. With the 
ambiguity on how the surface boundaries will resolve, highs in 
the 70s remain reasonable with lows generally ranging in the mid
40s to mid 50s.

&&

.AVIATION /06Z SATURDAY THROUGH WEDNESDAY/...
Through 06Z Sunday...Aviation challenge is timing and areal 
coverage of fog and associated LIFR/VLIFR this morning. Latest
GOES-19 fog product shows fog development near SLK and just
starting in the Winooski River Valley near MPV. Highest 
probability (90-100%) of IFR or lower conditions is at SLK/MPV 
with likely (65-75%) at EFK and chance (30-40%) at BTV/MSS. 
Have used prevailing group at SLK/MPV/EFK for fog, tempo at MSS
and just vcfg at RUT/BTV for now, as confidence is too low to 
mention IFR attm with light terrain driven winds under 5 knots.
Winds become southerly at 5 to 10 knots with localized gusts 14
to 20 knots expected at BTV/PBG and MSS by 15/16z. Ceilings
begin to lower toward MVFR conditions after 00z this evening
ahead of our next system.

Outlook...

Sunday: Mainly VFR, with local IFR possible. Chance SHRA, Slight
chance TSRA.
Sunday Night: Mainly VFR, with areas MVFR possible. Chance SHRA.
Monday: Mainly VFR, with local MVFR possible. NO SIG WX.
Monday Night: VFR. NO SIG WX.
Tuesday: VFR. NO SIG WX.
Tuesday Night: VFR. Chance SHRA.
Wednesday: Mainly VFR, with local MVFR possible. Slight chance
SHRA.

&&

.BTV WATCHES/WARNINGS/ADVISORIES...
VT...None.
NY...None.

&&

$$
